content.text: Prompt caching doesn't store Claude's answers. It stores the processed beginning of your prompt, up to a breakpoint, and reuses it when a later request starts with exactly the same content. Claude still generates every response from scratch, so output costs the same and identical questions can get different answers. What you save is input cost and latency, and only when the prefix is byte-identical.

A support team turns on prompt caching for its FAQ assistant and, in the same pull request, deletes the Redis cache of answers: "the API caches now." A week later, three surprises arrive together. The same question asked twice got two differently worded answers, one of them contradicting the help center. The output line of the bill didn't move. And
"Prompt caching stores Claude's responses, so sending the same question again returns a cached answer." For a web developer, that's the natural reading:

items.text: In web development, "cache" usually means stored responses: HTTP caches, CDNs, Redis in front of a slow query.
The parameter is called
cache_control
, like the HTTP header that governs response caching.
Send the same request twice with caching on and the second one is cheaper and starts answering sooner, which looks exactly like a cache hit on the answer.
Most explanations stop at "cached tokens are cheaper" without saying which tokens.

content.text: The half-truth: something really is reused, and it really does cut cost and latency. But it's the work of reading your input, not the work of writing the answer.
The cache holds your prompt's prefix
In the docs' words, prompt caching "references the entire prompt:
(in that order), up to and including the block designated with
. The cache key is a cryptographic hash of everything before and including it, so only a request whose prefix matches byte for byte can read the entry.
What's kept is the model's processed state for those tokens. The docs' data-retention note says that "

representations and cryptographic hashes are held in memory for the cache TTL." On a hit, the API uses that state instead of processing the prefix again, and works only on what comes after it. Then Claude generates the response the usual way, token by token. The docs are explicit: "Prompt caching has no effect on output token generation. The response you receive is identical to what you would get if prompt caching were not used."
So two identical questions produce two fresh generations. With caching or without, they can differ, and neither is "the cached answer."
Proof: a cache warmed with no answer at all
The docs describe pre-warming: send a request with
and the API reads your prompt, writes the cache at your breakpoint and returns at once, with an empty
array and zero output tokens billed. No answer exists, yet the next real request reads the cache. That only makes sense if the cache was never about answers.
What you pay, and what you don't

On Claude Opus 5.5, the pricing table lists base input at $4 per million tokens, a 5-minute cache write at $5, a 1-hour cache write at $8 and a cache hit at $0.20. Output stays at $20 per million, cached or not. The response's
for the prefix read from the cache,
for the prefix written now, and
for what comes after the last breakpoint. There's a throughput bonus too: for most models, cache reads don't count toward your input-tokens-per-minute rate limit.
Three rules from the docs explain most misses:

items.text: Writes happen only at your breakpoint. The system then looks back at most 20 blocks for entries earlier requests wrote; it never discovers stable content on its own.
Order matters:
tools
, then
system
, then
messages
. Changing a tool definition invalidates the whole cache.
Small prompts don't qualify. On Claude Opus 5.5 the minimum cacheable prompt is 512 tokens; shorter ones are processed without caching, and no error is returned.

content.text: That first rule is what broke the FAQ bot. Its system prompt began with the current time, and the breakpoint sat on that block, so every request wrote a new entry and no request ever read one:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import datetime

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def answer(question: str):
    now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC).isoformat()
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
        system=[{
            "type": "text",
            "text": f"Current time: {now}\n\n{FAQ_DOCUMENT}",  # new every call
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
        }],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    print("cache read:", reply.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)  # always 0


answer("How do I reset my password?")
answer("Can I change my plan mid-month?")

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import datetime

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def answer(question: str):
    now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC).isoformat()
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
        system=[{
            "type": "text",
            "text": FAQ_DOCUMENT,  # byte-identical on every call
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
        }],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Now: {now}\n\n{question}"}],
    )
    print("cache read:", reply.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)  # 0, then hits


answer("How do I reset my password?")
answer("Can I change my plan mid-month?")

content.text: The second version follows the docs' own advice: keep the system prompt a byte-stable constant and move per-request data into the user message, after the breakpoint. The first call writes the entry; every call within its lifetime reads it. Note what this does not fix: the two answers are still generated fresh.

The default entry lives 5 minutes, refreshed for free each time it's read, and the clock starts when the request starts, not when the response ends. A 1-hour lifetime costs twice the base input price to write. There's no way to clear the cache manually, and on the Claude API entries are isolated per workspace, so no other organization can ever read yours.

rows.text: It caches the processed prompt prefix; every response is generated fresh
Output generation is unaffected, so answers can still differ
It discounts input only; output costs the same
Only an identical prefix up to a breakpoint, at least 512 tokens on Opus 5.5
Entries stay until you clear them
5 minutes by default, refreshed on each hit, and you can't clear them

How to apply it in your project

Prompt caching makes reading your prompt cheaper. If you need the same answer for the same question, keep your own response cache, keyed on the normalized question and cleared when the source content changes.

items.title: Order the prompt from stable to volatile

content.text: Tools, then the system prompt, then documents, then per-request data. Put the breakpoint on the last block that's identical across requests.

items.title: Check the size and the timing

content.text: Make sure the cached prefix reaches your model's minimum, and use the 1-hour lifetime when requests are more than 5 minutes apart.
For batch jobs and parallel calls, write the cache once and let the rest read it.
per endpoint. A steady 0 means a prefix that changes; diagnostics tells you which part.

items.text: Prompt caching stores the processed prefix of your prompt, never Claude's response.
Every response is generated fresh, so output costs the same and answers can differ between identical requests.
A read needs a byte-identical prefix up to a breakpoint, in the order tools, system, messages.
On Claude Opus 5.5 the prefix needs at least 512 tokens, and entries last 5 minutes unless reused or set to 1 hour.
If you want reusable answers, build a response cache yourself.
